Grammar patrol:  An expletive is an exclamatory word or phrase, like "I'll be durned!", or "Golly!" Some expletives use bad words (like "Oh, sh*t!").  But not all bad words are expletives.  Some are nouns, some are adjectives, etc.  Some words can be used as expletives and ALSO as nouns or adjectives.  The bad word in this sentence, for instance is a subjective noun:  "That is bullsh*t".  Here, the bad word is an adjective: "She was f***ing hilarious."

Better to say "vulgarity" than "expletive", unless it really IS an expletive.

The custom of calling all bad words "expletives", I believe, started when transcriptions of the Nixon tapes (which were full of vulgarities), were published in newspapers, with the vulgarities deleted.  The transcribers kept typing "expletive deleted".

Legal jurisdiction vs internet freedom is not a difference, here. The question is specifically whether one country can claim to restrict what information is available to people living in other countries. That is a question of legal jurisdiction, which when answered affirmatively, becomes a problem for internet freedom.

Google operates in almost every country in the world. They abide by the laws of each country, but take the necessary position that government authority stops at its sovereign borders. If a Canadian court orders that certain information be removed from search results, then it is removed from search results for Canadians. If this is a problem (and in some ways it is), then an international treaty could set up a reciprocity system for countries with compatible legal systems.
